task_2.title: Drop Python 3.6 support
task_2.description: Version 2.5.0 removes Python 3.6 as a supported runtime. The provided release note makes this support-policy change explicit, and the supplied code diff shows no accompanying public API or runtime behavior changes for supported Python versions.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.5.0 drops support for Python 3.6 and treats Python 3.7 or newer as the supported interpreter range, without changing the library's user-facing behavior on still-supported Python versions.

expectation.grounded: The 2.5.0 upgrade should no longer advertise or support Python 3.6 as a valid runtime target. Users running supported Python versions should continue to observe the same public library behavior, because the provided code diff introduces no public API, exception, warning, or semantic runtime changes.
expectation.conceptual: The new release ends compatibility with Python 3.6. Apart from that interpreter support boundary, the upgrade should behave the same for users on supported Python versions.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new observable behavior changes in the library's public runtime surface beyond removing Python 3.6 from the supported environment contract. Existing behavior for supported interpreters should remain unchanged.
constraints.conceptual: Keep the upgrade narrowly scoped to supported-runtime policy. Users on supported Python versions should not need to adapt application behavior because of this release.

behavior: Python 3.6 is no longer part of the library's supported runtime matrix in version 2.5.0.
The provided code diff contains no public runtime API changes, indicating no new observable encode, decode, validation, warning, or exception behavior for supported Python versions.
The practical upgrade impact is compatibility-related: environments still on Python 3.6 fall outside the supported contract after upgrading.
acceptance_criteria: When evaluating version 2.5.0, it should be understood and documented as unsupported on Python 3.6.
When the library is used on Python 3.7 or newer, it should preserve the same observable runtime behavior exposed by version 2.4.0 unless changed elsewhere outside the provided diff.
When planning an upgrade from 2.4.0 to 2.5.0, teams should treat continued Python 3.6 usage as an incompatible environment for the new release.

task_1.title: Ignore unusable keys when loading JWK sets
task_1.description: Version 2.5.0 changes JWK Set loading so that incompatible or otherwise unusable keys are skipped instead of causing the entire load to fail, while invalid, empty, or wholly unusable key sets still raise an error.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that loading a JWK Set succeeds when the set contains at least one usable key, even if other entries are incompatible or unusable, and ensure that invalid, empty, or wholly unusable key sets are still rejected.

expectation.grounded: `PyJWKSet`, including creation through `PyJWKSet.from_dict` and `PyJWKSet.from_json`, should ignore individual keys that raise `PyJWKError` during `PyJWK` creation. If one or more keys are usable, `PyJWKSet.keys` should contain only those usable keys. The API should still raise `PyJWKSetError` when no keys are provided, when the `keys` value is not a list, or when every key in the list is unusable.
expectation.conceptual: When an application loads a JSON Web Key Set, unsupported or unusable entries should be skipped rather than aborting the whole load, as long as at least one valid key remains. Loading should still fail for invalid inputs, empty key sets, or key sets where none of the keys can be used.

constraints.grounded: Do not treat an unusable individual JWK entry as a hard failure if another entry can still be loaded successfully. Preserve `PyJWKSetError` as the observable failure type for invalid key-set inputs and for sets that produce zero usable keys after filtering.
constraints.conceptual: Be tolerant of mixed-quality key sets, but keep strict failure behavior for malformed inputs and for key sets that cannot provide any usable key.

behavior: `PyJWKSet` skips individual JWK entries that cannot be converted into `PyJWK` because they raise `PyJWKError`.
A mixed JWK Set containing both usable and unusable keys now loads successfully and exposes only the usable keys.
A JWK Set with no provided keys is rejected with `PyJWKSetError`.
A `keys` payload that is not a list is rejected with `PyJWKSetError`.
A JWK Set whose entries are all unusable is rejected with `PyJWKSetError` instead of producing an empty usable set.
acceptance_criteria: When a JWK Set contains both supported and unsupported or unusable keys, loading it should succeed and return only the usable keys.
When every key in a JWK Set is unusable, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError`.
When the JWK Set provides no keys, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError`.
When the `keys` member is not a list, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError`.

task_3.title: Warn on unsupported decode keyword arguments
task_3.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 starts surfacing deprecated misuse of JWT and JWS decode APIs by warning when callers pass unsupported extra keyword arguments, while keeping supported decoding and claim-validation parameters available as explicit arguments so existing decode flows remain compatible ahead of PyJWT 3.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT and JWS decode APIs warn callers when they pass unsupported extra keyword arguments, while continuing to accept documented decode and validation parameters without breaking current successful decode behavior in 2.5.0.

expectation.grounded: Calls to `decode()` and `decode_complete()` on the PyJWT and PyJWS decode APIs must continue to accept their explicit supported parameters, including `verify`, `detached_payload`, `audience`, `issuer`, and `leeway` where applicable. If additional unsupported keyword arguments are supplied through `**kwargs`, the call should emit `jwt.warnings.RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` naming the unsupported argument keys, but it should not reject the decode solely because those unsupported kwargs were present in version 2.5.0. A `decode()` call that internally uses `decode_complete()` should emit this deprecation warning only once for a single user call.
expectation.conceptual: The library should preserve successful decoding for supported inputs, but it should now clearly warn users when they rely on extra, non-supported keyword arguments so they can remove that usage before the next major release.

constraints.grounded: Do not convert unsupported extra kwargs into immediate hard failures in 2.5.0. Preserve runtime behavior for officially supported decode inputs such as detached payload handling and claim validation parameters. Compatibility only applies to documented decode arguments; callers and subclasses must not depend on arbitrary unknown kwargs being transparently forwarded through internal decode layers.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade should improve visibility into deprecated API usage without breaking normal decoding, and it should only preserve compatibility for supported public arguments rather than for accidental passthrough of custom extras.

behavior: Passing unsupported extra keyword arguments to PyJWT decode APIs emits a `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` and still allows the decode operation to proceed under current compatibility behavior.
Passing unsupported extra keyword arguments to PyJWS decode APIs emits a `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` and still allows the decode operation to proceed under current compatibility behavior.

Supported parameters that were previously often carried through `**kwargs` are exposed explicitly on PyJWT decode APIs for legacy verification control, detached payload decoding, and claim validation inputs such as audience, issuer, and leeway.
Detached payload support is exposed explicitly on PyJWS decode APIs rather than relying on arbitrary passthrough kwargs.
A `decode()` call no longer forwards arbitrary extra kwargs into `decode_complete()`, preventing duplicate deprecation warnings for the same unsupported user input.
Custom subclass integrations that relied on unknown kwargs flowing transparently through base decode methods can no longer assume that passthrough behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller uses only supported decode parameters, the token should decode with the same observable behavior as before and without a new unsupported-kwargs deprecation warning.

When a caller passes one or more unknown keyword arguments to `decode()`, the call should emit `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` identifying the unsupported argument name or names, and it should not fail solely because those extra kwargs were supplied.

When a caller passes one or more unknown keyword arguments to `decode_complete()`, the call should emit `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` identifying the unsupported argument name or names, and it should not fail solely because those extra kwargs were supplied.
When `decode()` delegates internally to `decode_complete()`, a single call with unsupported kwargs should produce one deprecation warning rather than duplicate warnings from both layers.

When callers provide supported explicit inputs such as `detached_payload`, `audience`, `issuer`, `leeway`, or legacy `verify` through the documented decode API parameters, those inputs should continue to participate in decoding and validation instead of being treated as unsupported extras.

task_4.title: Remove redundant wheel dependency metadata
task_4.description: Version 2.5.0 removes an unnecessary explicit `wheel` dependency from package metadata because the setuptools build backend already provides that build requirement. The change is a packaging cleanup intended to reduce redundant dependency declarations without changing runtime library behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.5.0 no longer requires or advertises `wheel` as an explicit project dependency, while preserving the existing install and build experience.

expectation.grounded: PyJWT 2.5.0 should stop declaring `wheel` as an explicit dependency in its package metadata because the setuptools build backend already adds the necessary wheel build support automatically. Based on the provided materials, no public runtime API, return value, warning, or exception behavior changes are introduced alongside this update.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should simplify packaging requirements by removing an unnecessary direct dependency, with no change to how developers use the library at runtime.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new runtime dependencies or alter existing PyJWT runtime semantics. Build and installation workflows supported by the setuptools backend must remain functional without the project explicitly listing `wheel` as a direct dependency.
constraints.conceptual: Keep the change limited to package dependency cleanup. Application behavior and normal library usage should remain unchanged.

behavior: The 2.5.0 package metadata no longer lists `wheel` as an explicit direct dependency.
Consumers building or installing the package through the supported setuptools backend continue to receive the necessary wheel build support without managing `wheel` as a declared project dependency.
No runtime-visible feature or API behavior changes are evidenced by the provided release note and code diff.
acceptance_criteria: When a consumer inspects the 2.5.0 package metadata, `wheel` is not present as a direct declared dependency.
When the package is built or installed using the supported setuptools build backend, the workflow still succeeds without requiring the project itself to declare `wheel` explicitly.
When an application upgrades from 2.4.0 to 2.5.0, existing runtime usage of the library continues to work unchanged based on the provided release-note and diff evidence.

task_5.title: Skip unusable keys when loading JWK sets
task_5.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 changes JWK set parsing so that a key set can still be loaded when it contains a mix of usable and unusable keys. Unusable entries are ignored instead of aborting the whole load, while invalid key-set containers and key sets with no usable keys still fail.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that loading a JWK Set does not fail just because some keys in the set are unusable, while still rejecting invalid key-set inputs and key sets that contain no usable keys.

expectation.grounded: When `PyJWKSet`, `PyJWKSet.from_dict`, or `PyJWKSet.from_json` processes a JWK Set whose `keys` collection contains both valid entries and entries that cannot be converted into `PyJWK`, the operation should succeed and retain only the usable keys. Entries that trigger `PyJWKError` during `PyJWK` construction should be skipped. A non-list `keys` value should still raise `PyJWKSetError`, a missing or empty `keys` collection should still raise `PyJWKSetError`, and a non-empty list that yields zero usable `PyJWK` objects should raise `PyJWKSetError` instead of returning an empty set.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to consume real-world JWK Sets that include unsupported or otherwise unusable keys without losing access to the valid keys in the same set. Loading should still fail when the key-set payload itself is malformed or when there are no usable keys to work with.

constraints.grounded: The change must preserve existing rejection of invalid JWK Set container shapes and empty key collections. It must not expose unusable entries through the resulting `PyJWKSet`, and it must continue to signal failure with `PyJWKSetError` when no usable keys remain after parsing.
constraints.conceptual: Be more tolerant of mixed-quality key sets, but do not silently accept malformed input or produce an empty usable key set as a successful result.

behavior: Parsing a JWK Set skips individual keys that are unusable for `PyJWK` construction instead of failing the entire load.
A successfully loaded `PyJWKSet` contains only the subset of keys that were usable.
If the `keys` field is not a list, JWK Set loading still fails with `PyJWKSetError`.
If the JWK Set has no keys or an empty `keys` collection, loading still fails with `PyJWKSetError`.
If the JWK Set provides a non-empty key list but every key is unusable, loading fails with `PyJWKSetError`.
acceptance_criteria: When a JWK Set contains at least one usable key and at least one unusable key, loading it through `PyJWKSet` APIs should succeed and expose only the usable keys.
When a JWK Set contains only unusable keys, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError`.
When the JWK Set payload provides a `keys` value that is not a list, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError`.
When the JWK Set payload omits keys or provides an empty `keys` collection, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError`.

task_6.title: Clarify JWT decode audience typing and supported kwargs
task_6.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 aligns the decode API contract for audience handling and related claim-validation arguments. The upgrade makes supported decode parameters explicit, warns when callers pass unsupported extra keyword arguments, and narrows the documented audience contract so applications rely on the public API instead of implicit passthrough behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT decoding in 2.5.0 exposes a consistent public contract for `audience` and other claim-validation arguments, so callers use explicit supported parameters, receive deprecation warnings for unsupported extra kwargs, and no longer treat bytes as a supported `audience` type.

expectation.grounded: `jwt.decode()` and `jwt.decode_complete()` should publicly accept `verify`, `detached_payload`, `audience`, `issuer`, and `leeway` as named parameters. Passing unsupported additional keyword arguments should emit `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` rather than silently behaving like a supported passthrough. `audience` should be treated as `str`, iterable of strings, or `None` in the supported API contract, while legacy `verify` should remain deprecated compatibility input whose mismatch with `options['verify_signature']` still warns.
expectation.conceptual: Applications upgrading to 2.5.0 should interact with JWT decoding through a clearer, explicitly supported parameter set. Audience validation should follow a documented string-or-string-list contract, and unsupported keyword passthrough should surface as deprecation warnings instead of remaining an implied feature.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress decode behavior for supported uses of `audience`, `issuer`, `leeway`, `detached_payload`, or `options['verify_signature']`. Keep accepting the legacy `verify` argument only for backward compatibility with warning semantics. Do not treat arbitrary extra kwargs as stable input to lower-level JWS decoding or claim validation.
constraints.conceptual: Existing supported decode flows should continue to work, but the library should narrow callers onto the documented API surface and avoid silently preserving unsupported keyword behaviors.

behavior: `jwt.decode()` and `jwt.decode_complete()` expose `verify`, `detached_payload`, `audience`, `issuer`, and `leeway` as explicit public parameters.
Passing unknown extra keyword arguments to either decode API emits `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` and identifies those kwargs as unsupported and deprecated.
Only `detached_payload` is forwarded to lower-level JWS decoding, and only `audience`, `issuer`, and `leeway` are forwarded into claim validation.
`audience` is defined in the supported API contract as a string, an iterable of strings, or `None`, instead of including bytes as a supported type.
Supplying `verify` with a value that conflicts with `options['verify_signature']` continues to emit the warning that the legacy `verify` argument has no effect in PyJWT 2.x.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller decodes a token with `audience` provided as a string or iterable of strings, decoding should use that value through the documented decode API.

When a caller provides `issuer`, `leeway`, or `detached_payload` to `jwt.decode()` or `jwt.decode_complete()`, those values should be accepted through explicit named parameters rather than requiring arbitrary kwargs passthrough.

When a caller passes an unsupported extra keyword argument to `jwt.decode()` or `jwt.decode_complete()`, the call should emit `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` instead of silently treating that argument as supported API.
When a caller passes `verify` and it disagrees with `options['verify_signature']`, decoding should emit the deprecation warning for the legacy `verify` argument.

When communicating the supported decode contract, `audience` should be represented as a string, an iterable of strings, or `None`, and callers should not rely on bytes being a supported audience type.

task_7.title: Improve PyJWKSet usable-key handling and validation errors
task_7.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 changes `PyJWKSet` loading so a JWK set can still be used when some individual keys are unusable, while set-level failures are reported more accurately for missing, empty, invalid, or fully unusable key collections.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `PyJWKSet` accepts JWK sets containing a mix of usable and unusable keys, reports set-level validation failures accurately, and only fails when the input does not provide keys, has an invalid key collection shape, or yields no usable keys.

expectation.grounded: `PyJWKSet` initialization, including construction through `PyJWKSet.from_dict` and `PyJWKSet.from_json`, should validate the `keys` payload at the set level and raise `PyJWKSetError` for missing or empty key collections, structurally invalid key collections, and collections whose members all fail `PyJWK` construction. When iterating supplied key entries, entries that raise `PyJWKError` during `PyJWK` creation should be ignored rather than aborting the entire set, provided at least one usable `PyJWK` remains.
expectation.conceptual: Loading a JWK set should succeed if the set contains at least one valid, usable key, even when some entries are unusable. Failures should clearly distinguish between an absent or empty key set, an invalid key-set shape, and a key set where every entry is unusable.

constraints.grounded: Do not reject a JWK set solely because one member cannot be materialized as `PyJWK`. Preserve successful loading of all usable keys. Continue to surface failures as `PyJWKSetError` at the set level when the key collection is absent, empty, not a valid list of key objects, or yields zero usable keys after filtering.
constraints.conceptual: Partial validity should be tolerated, but fully unusable or malformed sets must still fail. The behavior must not collapse different failure modes into the same generic outcome when users need to understand whether no keys were provided, the structure was wrong, or none of the keys could be used.

behavior: `PyJWKSet` skips individual key entries that fail `PyJWK` creation with `PyJWKError` instead of failing the whole load immediately.
A JWK set with both usable and unusable entries produces a `PyJWKSet` containing only the usable keys.
A missing or empty key collection raises `PyJWKSetError` as a no-keys condition rather than being treated as a generic invalid set.
A present but structurally invalid `keys` value raises `PyJWKSetError` as an invalid JWK set structure.
If every supplied key entry is unusable and filtered out, `PyJWKSet` raises `PyJWKSetError` because the set contains no usable keys.
acceptance_criteria: When a JWK set payload contains at least one key that can be loaded and one or more keys that cannot be loaded into `PyJWK`, loading the set should succeed and expose only the usable keys.
When the JWK set payload has no `keys` value or an empty `keys` collection, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError` for an empty or missing key set.
When the `keys` value is present but not a valid collection type for a JWK set, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError` for invalid set structure.

When every key entry in the provided `keys` collection is unusable, loading it should raise `PyJWKSetError` instead of returning an empty usable-key set or surfacing an individual-key failure as the final outcome.

task_9.title: Clarify runtime-specific exceptions for invalid JWS options
task_9.description: The 2.5.0 update clarifies existing behavior for invalid JWS option merging rather than introducing a production code change in the provided diff. When a non-dictionary `options` value is supplied to JWS APIs, the call remains invalid, but the observable exception may be `TypeError` or `ValueError` depending on the Python runtime, including PyPy3.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that invalid JWS `options` inputs are treated as caller errors without assuming a single exception type across Python runtimes.

expectation.grounded: For public JWS APIs that accept an `options` argument, including `PyJWS(...)` and `PyJWS.decode(...)`, passing a non-dict value must continue to fail during option merging. Consumers should treat both `TypeError` and `ValueError` as valid observable outcomes for this invalid input, with PyPy3 explicitly allowed to surface `ValueError`.
expectation.conceptual: When callers provide an invalid `options` value, the library should reject it as invalid input, while allowing the exact exception class to vary by supported Python runtime between `TypeError` and `ValueError`.

constraints.grounded: Do not reinterpret non-mapping `options` values as valid configuration, and do not narrow the documented failure mode to a single exception class when runtime-specific dict-unpacking behavior can emit either `TypeError` or `ValueError`.
constraints.conceptual: Invalid configuration must still fail fast, and the upgrade must preserve interpreter compatibility without promising one exact low-level exception type for this misuse.

behavior: Supplying a non-mapping object to the JWS constructor `options` parameter remains invalid and causes the call to fail before normal operation proceeds.
Supplying a non-mapping string to `PyJWS.decode(..., options=...)` remains invalid and causes failure during options processing.
Across supported Python runtimes, the observable exception for invalid option merging may be either `TypeError` or `ValueError` rather than one guaranteed class.
PyPy3 is explicitly within the supported behavior where invalid option merging can raise `ValueError`.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller passes a non-dictionary value to a JWS API `options` parameter, the call should fail instead of being accepted or coerced.
When the invalid `options` value is a string, the observable failure should be allowed to surface as either `TypeError` or `ValueError`, depending on the runtime.
Upgrading to 2.5.0 should not change valid `options` usage, but consumers that handled only `TypeError` for invalid `options` should treat `ValueError` as equally valid.

task_8.title: Align JWS decoding with PyJWT 2.5.0 API changes
task_8.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 updates the JWS API surface beyond typing cleanup by adding explicit algorithm lookup, making detached-payload decoding a supported parameter, and deprecating arbitrary extra kwargs during decode operations. The upgrade also tightens signature verification so missing or unsupported algorithms are rejected more consistently.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.5.0 preserves JWT/JWS decode behavior while adopting the new explicit JWS API: detached payloads must be passed through the supported decode parameter, arbitrary extra decode kwargs must no longer be relied on, and tokens with missing, disallowed, or unsupported algorithms must be rejected consistently.

expectation.grounded: The upgrade should align with the updated `PyJWS` contract: `PyJWS.decode` now supports an explicit `detached_payload` argument, `PyJWS.decode` and `PyJWS.decode_complete` emit `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` when additional unsupported kwargs are supplied, and `PyJWS.get_algorithm_by_name` provides public lookup of registered `Algorithm` instances. Signature verification should raise `InvalidAlgorithmError` when the header `alg` value is absent, falsy, not allowed by the caller-provided algorithms list, or cannot be resolved to a supported implementation.
expectation.conceptual: The library upgrade should expose a supported way to verify detached JWS payloads, warn consumers away from deprecated generic decode kwargs, and fail verification predictably whenever a token does not present a valid usable algorithm.

constraints.grounded: Do not depend on passthrough behavior for unknown kwargs in `decode` or `decode_complete`; only the supported parameters should affect decoding. Do not weaken existing algorithm allow-list enforcement or custom algorithm registration behavior. Unsupported algorithm resolution must surface through the documented warning and exception paths rather than silent fallback.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must preserve valid decoding flows while removing reliance on ambiguous decode inputs. It must remain strict about which algorithms are acceptable and must not silently accept tokens whose algorithm metadata is missing or unsupported.

behavior: `PyJWS.get_algorithm_by_name(name)` is available as a public lookup API and returns the registered algorithm object for supported names.
Looking up an unsupported algorithm, or one whose implementation is unavailable because required crypto support is missing, results in algorithm-resolution failure rather than a silent fallback.
`PyJWS.decode(..., detached_payload=...)` explicitly supports detached JWS verification without relying on arbitrary kwargs forwarding.

Passing extra unsupported keyword arguments to `PyJWS.decode` or `PyJWS.decode_complete` emits `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning`, signaling that this calling pattern is deprecated for removal in the next major version.

During signature verification, tokens whose header has no usable `alg` value, whose `alg` is not in the allowed algorithms list, or whose algorithm cannot be resolved are rejected with `InvalidAlgorithmError`.
acceptance_criteria: When decoding a detached JWS, callers can provide the detached body through the explicit `detached_payload` parameter and the token is evaluated using that payload.
When callers pass unknown extra keyword arguments to `decode` or `decode_complete`, the library emits `RemovedInPyjwt3Warning` instead of treating those kwargs as stable supported API.
When a token header omits `alg`, provides a falsy `alg`, or names an algorithm outside the allowed set, decoding fails with `InvalidAlgorithmError`.
When code requests an algorithm implementation by name through `get_algorithm_by_name`, supported names resolve to the registered algorithm object and unsupported names do not resolve silently.
When a token uses a supported allowed algorithm and its signature is valid, decoding continues to succeed under the updated API.

task_11.title: Correct EdDSA signing API documentation typo
task_11.description: The update corrects a typo in the EdDSA signing documentation so the accepted private key objects are described accurately. This is a documentation-only change intended to reduce confusion for users reading the API reference.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the EdDSA signing documentation correctly describes the accepted private key input types so users are not misled by a typo in the API reference.

expectation.grounded: The EdDSA signing API documentation in the jwt.algorithms module should describe the `key` parameter as an instance of either `Ed25519PrivateKey` or `Ed448PrivateKey`. The published API reference should use the correct Python term for an object of those types and should not suggest an invalid or misspelled term.
expectation.conceptual: Users reading the EdDSA signing documentation should see an accurate description of which private key objects are supported, using correct terminology that matches normal Python usage.

constraints.grounded: This update is documentation-only and must not change signing behavior, accepted key handling, return values, raised errors, or other runtime semantics of the EdDSA implementation.
constraints.conceptual: The change should improve clarity in the docs without altering how the library behaves in production.

behavior: The EdDSA signing documentation now refers to the private key argument using the correct term for an object instance.
The documented supported private key types for EdDSA signing remain `Ed25519PrivateKey` and `Ed448PrivateKey`.
No runtime behavior, API surface, or validation logic changes as part of this update.
acceptance_criteria: When a user reads the EdDSA signing API documentation, it should state that the signing key is an instance of `Ed25519PrivateKey` or `Ed448PrivateKey`.
When users consult the updated documentation, they should no longer encounter the typo in the private key type description.
Using the library at runtime should behave the same before and after this update because the change is limited to documentation.

task_10.title: Improve strict typing compatibility in jwt.utils
task_10.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 refines typing in jwt.utils so projects using Pyright strict mode do not inherit type-checking issues from the library, while preserving existing optional cryptography handling and SSH public key parsing behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.5.0 removes strict-mode type-checking issues in jwt.utils without changing the observable behavior of optional cryptography support or SSH public key format handling.

expectation.grounded: The jwt.utils module should be consumable under Pyright strict mode without library-originated typing failures. When the optional cryptography dependency is unavailable, jwt.utils should still import cleanly and represent the missing EllipticCurve symbol as an explicit absent value rather than a permissive fallback type. SSH public key pattern handling in jwt.utils should continue accepting the same byte-oriented OpenSSH public key inputs as before.
expectation.conceptual: Applications that use strict static type checking should be able to upgrade without adding local suppressions for library code, and existing runtime behavior for optional crypto support and SSH key recognition should remain unchanged.

constraints.grounded: Do not make jwt.utils require cryptography at import time, and do not change the accepted byte-format structure used for SSH public key parsing while resolving the typing issue.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade should improve developer tooling compatibility only; it must not force new runtime dependencies or alter the key formats that existing consumers already provide.

behavior: jwt.utils continues to support environments where cryptography is not installed, with the unavailable EllipticCurve symbol modeled as an explicit missing value instead of an unconstrained type placeholder.
Strict static analysis of code that imports jwt.utils should no longer report the library-side typing issue addressed in the 2.5.0 release.
SSH public key detection in jwt.utils remains byte-oriented and preserves the same observable matching behavior for supported OpenSSH public key inputs.
acceptance_criteria: When a project upgrades to PyJWT 2.5.0 and runs Pyright in strict mode against code that imports jwt.utils, the library should not introduce new strict-mode typing errors from that module.
When cryptography is not installed, importing jwt.utils should still succeed without requiring the optional dependency.
When supported OpenSSH public key byte strings are passed through the relevant jwt.utils parsing path, they should be recognized the same way as before the upgrade.

task_12.title: Correct documentation typo with no runtime behavior change
task_12.description: Version 2.5.0 corrects a published typo by changing an incorrect term to the intended word "prior". The provided code diff is empty, so this upgrade should be treated as a documentation-only correction with no user-visible runtime, API, or error-handling changes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the 2.5.0 upgrade corrects the published typo so documentation reads "prior" instead of the misspelled term, while preserving existing library behavior.

expectation.grounded: The release content should reflect the typo correction from the misspelled word to "prior". Because the provided code diff contains no changes, no public API names, callable behavior, return values, raised error types, warnings, or state transitions should change as part of this update.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2.5.0 should see corrected wording in the published documentation or release content, with no functional differences in how the library behaves at runtime.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce runtime changes that are unsupported by the provided evidence. Preserve existing API compatibility and observable behavior because no code-level modifications are present in the supplied diff.
constraints.conceptual: Treat this upgrade as editorial only. Existing integrations should continue to work exactly as before.

behavior: Published release or documentation text should use the correct word "prior" instead of the typo identified in the release note.
No runtime behavior change is evidenced by the provided code diff.
No public API, exception, warning, or state-management changes are evidenced by the provided code diff.
acceptance_criteria: When users view the affected release or documentation content in version 2.5.0, it should contain the corrected term "prior".
When existing applications upgrade from 2.4.0 to 2.5.0, they should observe no runtime or API behavior changes attributable to this update.
When users rely on prior integration behavior, the upgrade should remain non-breaking because no code changes are provided with this release item.

task_14.title: Add EC JWK export support to ECAlgorithm
task_14.description: Version 2.5.0 adds elliptic-curve JWK export support to the public algorithm API so applications can serialize EC public and private keys through ECAlgorithm, including supported curve identification and validation of unsupported key inputs.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to 2.5.0 can export elliptic-curve keys through the JWT algorithm API as JWKs, including supported public and private EC keys, while rejecting unsupported key objects and unsupported EC curves with a key-related error.

expectation.grounded: ECAlgorithm must expose a public to_jwk operation that accepts EllipticCurvePublicKey and EllipticCurvePrivateKey inputs and returns a JWK JSON representation with kty set to EC, the appropriate crv value, and the public point coordinates. When the input is a private EC key, the JWK must also include the private component. JWKs produced by ECAlgorithm.to_jwk should remain consumable by ECAlgorithm.from_jwk for supported curves.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to serialize supported EC keys into standard JWK form through ECAlgorithm, use the exported value anywhere a JWK is expected, and rely on the result to preserve the original key material needed for later JWK import.

constraints.grounded: Supported curve mappings are limited to P-256, P-384, P-521, and secp256k1. Inputs that are not EC public/private key objects, or EC keys using unsupported curves, must fail by raising InvalidKeyError instead of producing a partial or ambiguous JWK. Existing EC JWK import behavior via from_jwk must remain compatible with the exported format.
constraints.conceptual: The feature should only succeed for supported EC key types and named curves, fail clearly for unsupported inputs, and avoid changing how valid EC JWKs are interpreted on import.

behavior: ECAlgorithm gains JWK export support for elliptic-curve public keys.
ECAlgorithm gains JWK export support for elliptic-curve private keys.
Exported EC JWKs identify the key type as EC and include the curve name plus public coordinate values.
Exported EC JWKs include the private scalar only when the source key is private.
Supported curve names are emitted as P-256, P-384, P-521, or secp256k1 based on the source EC key.
Passing a non-EC key object to ECAlgorithm.to_jwk raises InvalidKeyError.
Passing an EC key on an unsupported curve to ECAlgorithm.to_jwk raises InvalidKeyError.
For supported EC keys, the JWK emitted by ECAlgorithm.to_jwk is compatible with ECAlgorithm.from_jwk round-trip import.
acceptance_criteria: When a supported EC public key is provided to ECAlgorithm.to_jwk, it should return a JWK JSON value describing the EC key type, curve, and public point coordinates.
When a supported EC private key is provided to ECAlgorithm.to_jwk, it should return a JWK JSON value that includes the same public key information plus the private component.
When the source key uses P-256, P-384, P-521, or secp256k1, the exported JWK should expose the matching standard curve identifier.
When a caller passes an object that is not an EC public or private key to ECAlgorithm.to_jwk, it should raise InvalidKeyError.
When a caller passes an EC key that uses an unsupported curve to ECAlgorithm.to_jwk, it should raise InvalidKeyError.
When a supported EC key is exported with ECAlgorithm.to_jwk and then imported with ECAlgorithm.from_jwk, it should preserve the original key semantics.

task_13.title: Deterministic JWT header ordering
task_13.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 fixes token-generation instability caused by JWT/JWS header key order. Tokens created from the same header content should now be serialized consistently so header ordering alone does not change the signed output.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that encoding a JWT with equivalent header content produces a stable result even when header fields are supplied in a different order.

expectation.grounded: Calls that encode JWS/JWT values, including `jwt.encode(..., headers=...)`, should serialize the protected header deterministically so semantically identical header dictionaries yield the same encoded header and signed token regardless of key insertion order.
expectation.conceptual: Token generation should treat header field ordering as non-semantic. If the header content is the same, the emitted token should not change just because the caller built the header object in a different order.

constraints.grounded: The set of emitted header parameters and existing signing behavior must remain compatible; the fix should remove order-only variation without introducing new required inputs, new warning/error behavior, or changes to the meaning of existing header values.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should preserve current JWT behavior and only eliminate instability caused by header ordering. Equivalent requests must stay equivalent, and non-order-related behavior must not regress.

behavior: JWT/JWS protected headers are encoded in a deterministic key order during token generation.
Equivalent header dictionaries produce the same protected-header representation even if their keys were inserted in different orders.
Because the protected header becomes stable, the final signed token no longer changes solely due to header key ordering.
acceptance_criteria: When a token is encoded twice with the same payload, algorithm, and header key/value pairs but the header keys are provided in different orders, it should produce the same token string.
When custom header parameters are supplied, token generation should continue to succeed and include the same semantic header content as before.
When header ordering is the only difference between two encode calls, the observable result should be stable rather than order-dependent.

task_15.title: Expose public algorithm lookup for JWT alg values
task_15.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 adds a public way to retrieve the Algorithm object associated with a JWT alg name, enabling advanced client-side workflows such as OIDC at_hash handling. The signing and verification paths were also aligned around the same lookup behavior so unsupported, missing, or disallowed algorithms are handled consistently through the library's public exceptions.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications can retrieve the Algorithm object for a JWT algorithm name through the public API for advanced token-processing workflows such as OIDC at_hash handling, while signing and signature verification continue to reject missing, unsupported, or disallowed algorithms with the appropriate public error behavior.

expectation.grounded: Expose `get_algorithm_by_name` on both the `PyJWS` API and the top-level `jwt` package so callers can resolve a string `alg` value to its `Algorithm` instance. For supported registered algorithms, the lookup should return the matching `Algorithm`. For unsupported algorithms, it should raise `NotImplementedError`; when the requested algorithm depends on cryptography support that is unavailable, the failure should still surface as `NotImplementedError`. `encode` should use the same effective algorithm resolution path, including header `alg` overrides, before key preparation and signing. `_verify_signature` should reject missing or non-allowed `alg` values with `InvalidAlgorithmError`, translate unsupported algorithm lookup failures into `InvalidAlgorithmError`, and continue to raise `InvalidSignatureError` only when verification runs and the signature check fails.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to ask the library for the algorithm object represented by a JWT's `alg` header and use that object in higher-level token validation flows. The library should preserve strict algorithm enforcement during signing and verification: unsupported or disallowed algorithms must fail clearly, and signature failures must remain distinct from algorithm-selection failures.

constraints.grounded: The new public lookup must respect the library's registered algorithm set and existing dependency boundaries. Exposing algorithm retrieval must not bypass allowed-algorithm filtering during verification, must not change header precedence when `encode` receives an overriding `alg` header, and must preserve the distinction between algorithm errors (`NotImplementedError` or `InvalidAlgorithmError`, depending on API surface) and signature-check failures (`InvalidSignatureError`).
constraints.conceptual: Making algorithm metadata accessible should not relax any security checks. Existing signing and verification behavior should remain strict about which algorithms are permitted, while continuing to report unsupported algorithms differently from bad signatures.

behavior: A new public `get_algorithm_by_name` lookup is available from both `PyJWS` and the top-level `jwt` API.
Looking up a supported algorithm name returns the corresponding `Algorithm` object.
Looking up an unsupported algorithm raises `NotImplementedError`; algorithms that require unavailable cryptography support also fail as `NotImplementedError` rather than returning a value.
Token encoding resolves the effective algorithm, including any `alg` header override, through the same algorithm lookup before preparing the key and producing a signature.
Signature verification now treats a missing or falsy `alg` header as an invalid/disallowed algorithm instead of proceeding with lookup.
Signature verification converts unsupported algorithm lookup failures into `InvalidAlgorithmError`, while a completed verification that does not match still raises `InvalidSignatureError`.
acceptance_criteria: When an application calls `jwt.get_algorithm_by_name` or `PyJWS.get_algorithm_by_name` with a supported algorithm name such as a registered JWT `alg`, it should receive the corresponding `Algorithm` object.
When an application calls the new lookup API with an unsupported algorithm name, it should receive `NotImplementedError` instead of a successful result.

When an application signs a token and the effective algorithm is determined by the function argument or an overriding header `alg`, the library should use that resolved algorithm for key preparation and signing.
When signature verification receives a token whose `alg` header is missing, empty, unsupported, or outside the caller's allowed algorithm list, it should fail with `InvalidAlgorithmError`.
When signature verification runs with a supported and allowed algorithm but the signature does not validate, it should fail with `InvalidSignatureError` rather than an algorithm-selection error.

task_17.title: Add TTL-based JWKS caching and refresh behavior to PyJWKClient
task_17.description: PyJWT 2.5.0 changes PyJWKClient so it caches the full JWK set for a configurable time window, refreshes that set when a requested key id is missing, and normalizes JWKS fetch failures into library errors. The update also changes defaults by enabling JWK set caching and making per-key LRU caching opt-in.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that PyJWKClient uses a bounded, configurable JWK set cache for signing-key resolution, refreshes the JWK set when a requested kid is missing, and exposes the new cache controls and error behavior introduced in PyJWT 2.5.0.

expectation.grounded: PyJWKClient should accept the public constructor options cache_jwk_set and lifespan, with JWK set caching enabled by default for 300 seconds and rejected with PyJWKClientError when lifespan is not greater than zero. get_jwk_set(refresh=False) and get_signing_keys(refresh=False) should reuse a non-expired cached JWK set unless refresh is requested or cache_jwk_set is disabled. get_signing_key(kid) should retry once against a freshly fetched JWK set when no matching kid exists in the current set, and then raise PyJWKClientError if the kid is still unresolved. URL fetch failures during JWKS retrieval should surface as PyJWKClientError, and a failed fetch or refresh should clear the stored JWK set cache. cache_keys should remain available but disabled by default unless explicitly enabled.
expectation.conceptual: The JWKS client should reuse recently fetched signing-key metadata for a short configurable period, bypass or refresh that cache when asked, and recover from key rotation by refetching once before failing. Fetch failures should be reported consistently through the library's error type, and stale cached JWKS data should not remain after a failed refresh.

constraints.grounded: Do not return expired cached JWK set data. Do not keep JWK set caching active when cache_jwk_set is false. Do not silently accept a zero or negative JWKS cache lifespan when JWK set caching is enabled. Keep unresolved kid failures observable as PyJWKClientError after the allowed refresh attempt. get_signing_key_from_jwt should inherit the updated signing-key lookup behavior through get_signing_key.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must preserve correct signing-key resolution while preventing indefinite reuse of stale JWKS data. Applications must be able to disable set-level caching or explicitly re-enable key-level caching, and missing-key failures must still be surfaced when a refresh cannot resolve them.

behavior: PyJWKClient should cache the fetched JWK set by default and reuse it across repeated JWK set and signing-key lookups within the configured lifespan.
The JWK set cache should expire after the configured lifespan in seconds, defaulting to 300 seconds.
Passing refresh=true to get_jwk_set or get_signing_keys should bypass the cached JWK set and fetch a new one.
When get_signing_key(kid) does not find a matching key in the current JWK set, it should fetch a fresh JWK set once and retry the lookup before failing.
When a JWKS URL fetch fails, the client should raise PyJWKClientError and clear any stored JWK set cache entry.
Per-key cache_keys caching should be opt-in rather than enabled by default.
Constructing PyJWKClient with JWK set caching enabled and a non-positive lifespan should raise PyJWKClientError.
acceptance_criteria: When a client performs repeated JWK set or signing-key lookups within the default cache window and does not request a refresh, it should reuse the previously fetched JWK set instead of refetching it.
When cache_jwk_set is set to false, repeated JWK set retrievals should not reuse an internal JWK set cache.
When the configured JWK set cache lifespan has elapsed, the next JWK set or signing-key lookup should fetch a fresh JWK set before returning results.
When get_signing_key(kid) does not find the requested kid in the current JWK set but that key exists in a newly fetched JWK set, the lookup should succeed after one refresh attempt.
When get_signing_key(kid) still cannot find the requested kid after refreshing the JWK set, it should fail with PyJWKClientError.
When JWKS retrieval fails because the remote URL request cannot be completed, the operation should fail with PyJWKClientError and the stored JWK set cache should no longer contain the old data.
When lifespan is zero or negative while JWK set caching is enabled, PyJWKClient construction should fail with PyJWKClientError.
When cache_keys is not explicitly enabled, repeated get_signing_key(kid) calls should not rely on per-key LRU caching behavior.

task_16.title: Complete typing support for jwt.help
task_16.description: The 2.5.0 update completes typing coverage for the public `jwt.help` helper module and adds the missing cryptography type dependency for typed environments. This is intended to improve static analysis and package completeness without changing the helper's runtime behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.5.0 provides complete type-checker support for the `jwt.help` helper APIs and includes the missing cryptography type information needed to analyze those APIs cleanly in typed projects.

expectation.grounded: The public `jwt.help.info()` API should expose an explicit typed contract indicating that it returns a nested mapping of string keys and values describing the runtime environment, and `jwt.help.main()` should expose a `None` return contract. Typed consumers should be able to analyze `jwt.help` without needing local suppressions for the optional `cryptography` import or for the PyPy-specific version branch, and installations that rely on typing metadata should include the missing `cryptography` stub dependency.
expectation.conceptual: The library should present `jwt.help` as a fully typed public helper module. Developers using IDEs and static type checkers should be able to inspect and use its helper functions with accurate signatures and without extra workaround configuration, while the observable runtime output stays the same.

constraints.grounded: The upgrade must preserve the existing purpose and observable output of `jwt.help.info()` and `jwt.help.main()`, including support for environments where `cryptography` is unavailable and for PyPy version reporting. The change must not introduce new runtime requirements, error conditions, or altered JSON content beyond typing metadata and packaging completeness.
constraints.conceptual: This should be a non-breaking typing improvement. Existing consumers should continue to get the same helper behavior and environment reporting, with the only meaningful change being better typing support and dependency completeness for typed development workflows.

behavior: `jwt.help.info()` now has an explicit public return type describing a nested string-to-string mapping of environment metadata.
`jwt.help.main()` now has an explicit public return type indicating that it only prints the formatted helper output and does not return a value.
The helper module remains importable and usable when `cryptography` is not installed, while its optional import is represented in a type-checker-friendly way.
The PyPy-specific implementation version handling is expressed in a way that preserves the same reported version semantics while making the branch analyzable by static type checkers.
Typed installations include the missing cryptography stub dependency so consumers analyzing the package have the necessary type information available.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer inspects or type-checks `jwt.help.info()`, it should be recognized as returning structured environment metadata rather than an untyped value.
When a developer inspects or type-checks `jwt.help.main()`, it should be recognized as a procedure that returns no value.
When the library is used in a typed project, analyzing `jwt.help` should not require suppressing missing cryptography type information that the package is expected to provide.
When `cryptography` is absent at runtime, `jwt.help` should remain usable and continue reporting helper information without introducing a new import failure.
When running under PyPy, the helper should continue to report the interpreter version in the same observable format while remaining compatible with static analysis.
